newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Wool International casts doubt on wool price surge.
newsitem.headline: Wool International casts doubt on wool price surge.

text.p: Australia's wool stockpile marketing authority Wool International (WI) cast doubt over whether wool prices could sustain their recent surge.
"Wool prices are now up sharply, some would say they have risen too quickly," Bob Richardson, WI's chief executive, told the Wool Council of Australia annual conference on Thursday.
"WI continues to appraise the situation in a context of maximising value for all wool sold," he said.
"Given the continued weak economic and retail situation in some important markets, it remains to be seen how durable the recent price rises will be," he said.
The Australian eastern market indicator rose 25 cents at this week's auctiuons to 700 cents a kg clean, its highest level since early September 1995.
Wool was in a dilemma with prices too high to gain market share but too low to stimulate a return of productive resources, Richardson added.

Forecasting an average eastern indicator of 640 cents a kg for the 1997/98 season, Richardson said continued attractive returns in cropping industries suggested no economic incentive for sheep numbers to increase in over the next two years.

The average eastern indicator for this season ending June 30 now seemed likely to be slightly above WI's original forecast of 600 cents a kg but still below last season's average of 619 cents, he said.
Strongest demand has been in finer micron categories with renewed buying from Japan and Western Europe.
Trade clearances of auction sales plus WI's deliveries were up sharply this season by 14 percent on low 1995/96 figures.

Total trade clearances were expected to rise marginally by two percent next season to around 790 million kgs with increased sales from grower-held stocks, presently estimated at higher than normal levels of around 730,000 bales or 129 million kgs.

But WI's assesment was for only a limited improvement in underlying consumer demand outlook, he said. In the major high unit value markets of Japan, Germany and Italy, retail sales of wool were expected to be static at the lower levels of 1996.
The most positive markets continued to be the U.S. and Britain, supported by growth in newly industrialising Asian economies other than China and South Korea, he said.
But the wool-to-synthetic fibre price ratio was the highest in more than six years, at 3.4, he said.

"This presents something of a dilemma for wool; it is caught in the crossfire between a price too high to gain market share in a competitive low growth fibre market and too low to stimulate some shift of resources from cropping back to grazing that may be required in three years time when the stockpile is gone," he said.
Richardson said the wool stockpile was now down to 1.7 million bales or 35 percent of its peak in 1991.
Substantial uncertainties accompanied WI's forecast of an average 640 cents price for 1997/98, Richardson said.

"It implies some seasonal softening in prices in the September-December period compared to recent weeks. If prices seemed likely to significantly exceed this level, WI sales could rise above the presently assumed level of about 100 million kgs for next season," he said.
Australia's wool stockpile debt was now down to about A$700 million, or 26 percent of its starting level, he also said.
-- Michael Byrnes Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
